topic: Commercialisation I: Startup vs traditional, lean startup, agile

questions.stem: Steve Blank defines a startup as:
choices: Any small business with fewer than 50 employees.
A temporary organisation in search of a repeatable, scalable, profitable business model.
A company that has raised venture capital.
A technology company in its first year.
questions.explanation: Blank's definition is exam-critical: a startup is in SEARCH of a business model. Once the model is found, it stops being a startup.

questions.stem: The Build-Measure-Learn loop is most associated with:
questions.explanation: Ries codified the BML loop in The Lean Startup, drawing on Blank's Customer Development and Toyota's lean manufacturing.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST definition of an MVP (Minimum Viable Product)?
choices: A polished version 1 of the product.
The smallest product that lets you complete one Build-Measure-Learn loop with minimum effort and time.
A finished product launched to a small market.
The first feature of the product.
questions.explanation: An MVP is defined by its function: to enable validated learning with the minimum waste. Polish and feature count are secondary.

questions.stem: A 'Wizard of Oz' MVP is one in which:
choices: The product appears automated to users but humans run the back-end manually.
Users design their own version of the product.
The product is delivered in three colours only.
Users vote on which features to build next.
questions.explanation: Wizard of Oz MVPs preserve the user experience while avoiding the cost of automation — validating demand before investing in engineering.

questions.stem: Instagram's origin from the check-in app Burbn is best described as which type of pivot?
choices: Zoom-in pivot (a sub-feature becomes the whole product)
questions.explanation: Burbn had photo-sharing as one of many features. Zooming in on just that one feature produced Instagram — Ries's canonical zoom-in pivot.

questions.stem: Steve Blank's Customer Development has four stages. They are:
questions.explanation: The four Blank stages: Customer Discovery, Customer Validation, Customer Creation, Company Building. Stages 1-2 are 'search'; 3-4 are 'execution'.

questions.stem: Which is a key failure mode of traditional product development for startups?
choices: Too much customer interaction during product development.
Building a fully featured product against an untested spec and discovering after launch that the market does not want it.
questions.explanation: Traditional product development assumes market validity. Lean startup makes market validation continuous — the hardest startup question is 'do they want it', not 'can we build it'.

questions.stem: After a Build-Measure-Learn loop, a team that finds data invalidating its key hypothesis should:
choices: Persevere with the same plan; the data will improve with time.
Pivot — a structured course correction keeping one foot in what worked, moving the other somewhere new.
questions.explanation: Pivot vs persevere is the explicit decision after each BML loop. Pivots are structured, not panicked — they preserve learnings while changing direction.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of Ries's three engines of growth?
questions.explanation: Sticky, viral, and paid are the three engines. Geographic expansion is a channel/strategy, not an engine of growth in Ries's framework.

questions.stem: Slack famously pivoted from:
choices: A multiplayer game (Glitch) — internal comms tool spun out and became the product
questions.explanation: Stewart Butterfield's team built internal comms while making Glitch. When the game failed, the internal tool was the surviving product. A famous pivot story.

questions.stem: Dropbox's famous demo VIDEO before product launch was an example of:
choices: A smoke-test / explainer-video MVP designed to validate demand before building the technically hard cross-platform sync.
questions.explanation: Dropbox shipped a video demo and watched the beta waitlist swell. They validated demand cheaply before tackling the engineering.

questions.stem: Lean Startup is most APPROPRIATE in conditions of:
choices: Stable, known markets with known products.
Extreme uncertainty about customer, product, and business model.
questions.explanation: Lean startup is a methodology for extreme uncertainty. Stable, known contexts are better served by traditional planning and execution.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a typical pivot type in Ries's taxonomy?
questions.explanation: Ries names zoom-in, zoom-out, customer-segment, customer-need, platform, business-architecture, engine-of-growth, channel, and technology pivots. Marketing-spend is not one of them.

questions.stem: Innovation accounting in Lean Startup means:
choices: Filing tax returns for an early-stage startup.
Tracking cohort-based metrics that show whether the engine of growth is improving over time.
questions.explanation: Innovation accounting replaces traditional revenue/profit metrics in early stages with cohort metrics that reveal whether learning is converging.

questions.stem: The Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder) has how many blocks?
questions.explanation: Nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, cost structure.

questions.stem: Agile development and Lean Startup are related in that:
choices: They are the same methodology under different names.
Agile is how engineering ships iteratively; Lean Startup is how the whole business validates market hypotheses iteratively. They complement.
Agile is for software; Lean Startup is for hardware.
Agile predates Lean Startup by decades.
questions.explanation: Both share short cycles and feedback. They operate at different scopes — engineering execution vs business hypothesis testing. They combine well.

questions.stem: Why would a founder choose a Wizard of Oz MVP over a fully automated MVP?
choices: It defers engineering work until the value proposition is validated; the team learns without committing to automation that may never be needed.
It is required for regulatory approval.
questions.explanation: Wizard of Oz defers automation cost, lets the team observe user behaviour, and avoids building features that customers may not value.

questions.stem: Which is the MOST APPROPRIATE engine of growth for a B2B SaaS product with low natural virality but strong retention?
choices: Hybrid of all three at once
questions.explanation: Sticky engine: low churn drives net growth even with modest acquisition. B2B SaaS often optimises retention (NPS, NRR) before scaling acquisition.

questions.stem: Which is a strong argument that Lean Startup does NOT work for deep biotech / hardtech?
choices: Long, capital-intensive, regulated development cycles make rapid MVP-driven Build-Measure-Learn loops infeasible; an mRNA vaccine cannot be shipped to 'see if customers like it'.
questions.explanation: Lean works best where iteration is cheap and fast. Biotech, fusion, aerospace, and similar hard-tech contexts require capital-heavy de-risking before any customer test.

questions.stem: Customer Discovery (Blank stage 1) is primarily about:
choices: Getting out of the building to interview prospective customers and validate the problem and value proposition.
questions.explanation: Stage 1 is hypothesis-testing on the problem and customer. Founders interview, observe, and refine — no scaling yet.

questions.stem: A founder spends nine months building a polished mobile app, then launches and watches downloads stall at 200 users with eight months runway. The MOST appropriate lean-startup response is:
choices: Spend the remaining budget on marketing.
Run customer interviews with users and non-users to identify the failed leap-of-faith hypothesis; consider a structured pivot (zoom-in, segment, channel); reduce burn to preserve optionality.
Raise more capital to extend the launch campaign.
questions.explanation: The textbook lean response: diagnose what failed, pivot if needed, reduce burn, preserve runway for learning. More marketing on an unvalidated product wastes capital.

questions.stem: A 'concierge MVP' (e.g. Food on the Table) is one in which:
choices: The product is automated end-to-end from day one.
The founders manually deliver the service to a small number of users to learn what to build before automating.
Concierges in luxury hotels test the product.
Customers pay a premium for personalised onboarding.
questions.explanation: Concierge MVPs prioritise learning over automation. Food on the Table founders personally helped families plan meals before automating the recommendation engine.

questions.stem: Which best contrasts Lean Startup with traditional product development on the HYPOTHESES dimension?
choices: Both make explicit hypotheses and test them.
Traditional product development bakes implicit untested hypotheses into the business plan; Lean Startup makes hypotheses explicit and tests them via experiments.
Traditional product development uses no hypotheses; Lean Startup does.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis difference is exam-critical: traditional plans treat assumptions as facts; lean treats them as testable hypotheses with falsification criteria.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument FOR a five-year business plan in some contexts?
choices: In mature firms entering known markets with known products, a detailed plan is useful for execution coordination — Lean Startup is not always the right tool.
It eliminates the need for customer discovery.
questions.explanation: Lean is for uncertainty. Mature firms in known markets benefit from traditional planning. Choosing the right tool to the context is part of senior judgement.

questions.stem: Which best summarises 'validated learning'?
choices: Customers saying they like the product in interviews.
Empirical evidence — typically behaviour, not opinion — that demonstrates the team has discovered valuable truths about its present and future business prospects.
questions.explanation: Validated learning is Ries's anchor concept: behaviour-based evidence about the business, not opinions, not vanity metrics. Cohort retention beats survey responses.
